    #135058. The 6 Best Gaming Headsets for All Types of Players

    📅 28 Apr 2025 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1803 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

    The 6 Best Gaming Headsets for All Types of Players

    📅 28 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nothing truly makes me feel immersed in a game the same way good sound does.
    • If you consider gaming your main hobby, you’re probably either a single-player person or you like to squad up in your battle royale of choice.
    • There are actually plenty of good headsets and trustworthy brands that make dozens of similar options.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nothing truly makes me feel immersed in a game the same way good sound does. And it’s impossible to get that level of tension in a horror game like Resident Evil, or the feeling of being absolutely locked in a competitive shooter without a good pair of headphones. Nowadays, video games are fully open world of 3D and spatial audio, and there's never been a better time to hop on the bandwagon. It's time to get a gaming headset.

    If you consider gaming your main hobby, you’re probably either a single-player person or you like to squad up in your battle royale of choice. It doesn’t matter, actually, because the only proper way to experience both ends of the gaming spectrum is with a headset. For single-player, that means fully immersive audio. For multiplayer, you’ll sound crystal clear to your teammates—no more confusion or excuses. The good noise-canceling headsets even have transparency modes so you don’t have to ignore everyone in your real life either.

    Here's the problem. There are actually plenty of good headsets and trustworthy brands that make dozens of similar options. Finding the headset that will work for you isn’t made to be easy, but that’s why I’m here. I know my gaming headsets like the back of my hand—that’s my job. To figure out if you need a high-end wireless SteelSeries headset, or if you’ll be happy with a sub-$100 option, read on. Hell, maybe you’d prefer earbuds. I’ve accounted for all options.

    This is the one gaming headset I won’t (and frankly can’t) say anything negative about. I suppose that’s what $600 gets you. SteelSeries has long made comfortable headsets that support multiple platforms with easy swapping. It introduced the world to its GameHub base station, letting you connect all your systems to one panel and easily control them all from there.

    It has been revealed that the Nova Elite takes every already perfectly solved puzzle piece and puts a little extra sheen on it. First off, it is gorgeous, with exteriors made from premium steel, aluminum, and vegan leather. Nothing else in the gaming space compares to it in terms of the luxe look. In terms of fit, the Nova Elite distributes its weight evenly so you can play for hours without discomfort.

    Recent findings suggest that and this headset’s gaming hub has an extra feature that really changes things. The hot-swappable batteries are SteelSeries’ biggest innovation in recent years, and here the hub also acts as a charger for your second (included) headset battery. So whichever one is not powering your current session is being charged. What this means is battery life is a solved problem. You literally never have to worry about running out of charge mid-game again. And for some, that alone might be worth the price of admission.

    Recent findings suggest that okay, forget what I just mentioned. This is everything a wireless headset needs to be for the average gamer. ASUS has targeted a lower price point and succeeded in terms of knowing which features to cut, and what to keep to make it still feel like a high-quality experience. You don't get active noise cancellation or the ability to play audio from two sources at once. For those luxuries, go for the Delta II.

    In a recent development, at 0.7 pounds, the Pelta is remarkably light and the furthest thing from bulky. It's about letting you play all day on those summer Saturdays where it's too hot to go outside. Where it surprises in this regard is battery life. Offering up to 70 hours between charges and a fit that won't leave you itchy and sweaty, this is the all-nighter-friendly headset.

    Recent findings suggest that while I wouldn't personally spring for a wired headset, those who do are hard to convince otherwise. And that crowd has spent the last couple of years rallying around the HyperX Cloud Alpha. If competitive gaming is the reason you are turning to a headset, this has everything you need for under $100.

    Sources indicate that you aren't going to get the audio options you do from the multi-hundred-dollar headsets SteelSeries and Corsair sell. Instead, you are paying a reasonable price for a high-quality microphone, and a comfortable pair of headphones. Stop worrying about lag and stop worrying about your headset running out of battery. It's time to wire in.

    Industry observers note that when it comes to sound quality, the Corsair Virtuoso Max brings it to a upcoming level. This is a better-sounding headset than most of the readers of this article have ever experienced.

    My favorite high-tech touch that we actually use is the simultaneous connection. Using the 2.4 GHz dongle and Bluetooth in tandem you can get the audio from your game and audio from a Bluetooth source at the same time. That means pumping in your own tunes or a background podcast while grinding levels. When playing with friends, I love the addition of a physical, sturdy, functional mic mute button.

    Industry observers note that the only issue is long-term comfort. Weighing in at just under a pound, the 60-hour battery life on the headset is a bit of a moot point. You'll want to take it off anyway because it can start to feel quite hard on your skull after a couple hours of white knuckle gaming.

    Sources indicate that if you have a single gaming machine and that console is a PS5, this is the headset I recommend. It is remarkably lightweight, weighing even less than the wired-only pair I recommended earlier, and it’s super easy to use—with a satisfying mute button that pops in and out, and a microphone that is entirely detachable. So if you’re settling in for a night of solo horror gaming, you can set the mic aside and still enjoy the excellent sound and spatial audio options. And if you know that battery is low, or you really just want the easiest solution, the package includes a 3.5mm cable for wired connection. Just plug that right into your DualSense controller and you’re off to the races.

    Industry observers note that beyond just PlayStation diehards, this is an excellent option for any PC or Nintendo gamer who wants a light wireless headset. It is fully compatible via USB-C transceiver or headphone cable with any other modern console, sans the Xbox.

    Okay, so I lied. When you clicked on this for the six best headsets, yeah one of these isn't a gaming headset at all. It's a set of earbuds designed by SteelSeries to be used on gaming consoles and it's as much of a game-changer as it sounds. If you feel cheated, don't fret. There are two more headsets listed in the honorable mentions below. Please accept my humble offering.

    According to recent reports, if you’ll allow me to talk about them for just a minute though, the Arctis GameBuds are just shy of a miracle. They are comfy earbuds with all-encompassing noise-canceling (gasp!), spatial audio support, and a very useful transparency/talk-through mode. The sound isn't quite on par with SteelSeries's larger headsets, but it still impresses. Plus, unlike the rest of these headsets, you can fit them in your pocket.

    SteelSeries Arctis Nova 7 ($179): You don't need to shell out for the Nova Elite to get a good Arctis headset. This one uses a simple USB-C dongle, so isn't nearly as complicated to set up, either.

    Turtle Beach Stealth Pro 2: ($349): My favorite new headset of the year. An excellent multi-platform choice with high-quality playback and call audio. It also uses a swappable battery system, so you never run out of charge in a heated gaming moment.

    What We Look for in a Gaming Headset.

    In a recent development, testing gaming headsets really isn't too difficult. You make sure it's compatible with what it says on the box, and then tell the people if it’s comfortable and if it sounds good. Shit simple until you do it enough to realize a simple truth. Most models from reputable brands are worth their costs, and very few companies have duds in their lineups. That noted, there are ways to tell what's going to rise from the crop. Here's some pointers for the next time you shop for headsets.

    Comfort — If you can't stay comfortable in them for more than an hour they are going straight in the trash. Even the most uncomfortable among these picks are still in the top 5% of comfortable gaming headphones.

    Sound Quality — Like with the pair of headphones you use to listen to music, you want clear sound with plenty of range.

    According to recent reports, microphone — If you're gaming online, your microphone needs to cut out unwanted background noise. Some offer noise cancelling, some just have good unidirectional builds. All on this list are great in this department.

    Recent findings suggest that directional Sound — Spatial audio is cool when watching movies, but when playing games this can take your team play to the next level. When you hear an enemy's footsteps, you can know they're behind you at four o'clock, not six. And that makes you an asset. It also makes the taste of victory that much sweeter.

    Connection — I will discuss wireless vs. wired shortly, but when it comes to the going wireless there's usually two ways to connect a gaming headset. Bluetooth or via a USB dongle. The latter typically has less latency and is the preferred way to connect.

    Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs).

    Are wired or wireless headsets better for gaming?

    If you care about latency (aka lag), we are going to recommend wired over wireless. The added hassle of wireless charging and connecting doesn't necessarily make up for the hassle of having a wire. Plus, you don't have to worry about it not working on some devices—which you do with pretty much every wireless device you buy.

    Do all gaming headsets work across all platforms?

    I'm glad you asked. No! As you may have noticed, there tend to be two kinds of headsets. Those that work with Xbox.. and those that work with everything else. Since Xbox uses its own wireless standard instead of Bluetooth. In practice, this means Xbox gamers need to be extra careful when buying headsets to make sure the one they're getting is compatible. SteelSeries, for example, sells two versions of each headset, one marked for Xbox.

    It's actually more complicated than "all headsets that work with PC also work with PlayStation and you have to get ones especially for Xbox," but in many of these cases that is the gist. Although the PlayStation headsets work on PC and Mac but not Nintendo Switch. So, yeah, it's pretty inconsistent. Seriously, just read the list of compatible platforms before you buy a headset.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that sometimes celebrities create trends, and sometimes celebrities wear trends. But then there are times when you really can’t tell which happened first. It’s a chicken-or-the-egg situation. That’s what we have on our hands with the leopard-print coat trend.

    Here’s the fact: Inde Navarrette, Elizabeth Debicki, and Michelle Randolph all wore leopard coats last week. Three of anything make a trend, especially A-list spottings. Also true: Leopard coats never really go out of style, so I’m not sure how much credit we can actually give the stars. But you can get Navarrette’s exact Rixo coat and Randolph’s from Aflalo.

    In case you feel compelled to make the trend your own, let me break it down a little further. Your leopard-print coat can—but doesn’t have to be—faux fur. It could also be more of a trench coat-like material or even jacquard. Many of the styles we’re seeing this season are collarless, but that’s simply a matter of preference.

    According to recent reports, really, I can’t think of a better fall/winter item. Pair your coat with a white tee and blue denim for a look that is as polished and cool as they come. Alternatively, layer up in your finest party attire for the holiday season. Even worn with a little black dress, this trend will make a statement.

    Whether you’re looking for a designer investment piece or an under-$400 option, I’ve found all the best leopard coats to browse now.

    The best designers know when and where to shop at most home decor stores. For example, IKEA suits tight budgets and DIY-friendly spaces, while Anthropologie is perfect for a whiff of whimsy. However, if you want to treat yourself to some sleek, splurge-worthy pieces, consider this your sign to mosey over to Design Within Reach, or DWR.

    In a recent development, since its founding in 1998, DWR has been the ultimate resource for buying midcentury and modern pieces. Though its physical and digital shelves are stocked with iconic contemporary furniture like the Eames Lounge Chair and Eero Saarinen’s Tulip Table, it’s possible to pick up some great wares without the astronomical sticker shock.

    Recent findings suggest that to help find high design for a great value, we asked several designers about the DWR items they reach for time and time again. Best of all? Everything’s under $1,000, so you won’t have to completely break the bank to treat yourself.

    It has been revealed that “One of my favorite things to purchase from DWR—whether as a gift for a client, friend, or a treat for myself—is Flamingo Estate’s candles. My go-to scents are the Tuscan Rosemary in the fall, Agrigento Olive Tree for any time of year, and Heirloom Tomato for any of my gardening friends and family. Beautifully packaged and incredibly clean-burning, these are a must!”—Darci Hether, founder of Darci Hether Fresh York.

    “We recently used the Fin bedside tables in a client’s home in Sag Harbor. I love how the pill-shaped silhouette softens the whole bedside setup. There are so many straight lines in a bedroom, and that one curve on either side of the bed gave the room a little personality while keeping it calm. I could see them working just as easily in a more tailored city bedroom as they do in a relaxed Hamptons home.” —Sarah Tract of Sarah Tract Interiors.

    It has been revealed that “We love to incorporate the Seine Portable Lamp into our designs for its beautiful balance of form and function. The textured glass casts a soft, ambient glow, while the antique brass detailing adds a timeless, sophisticated touch. Its cordless design makes it incredibly versatile, perfect for creating an intimate atmosphere on a dining table, bookshelf, or anywhere a little extra warmth is needed. It's one of those small details that makes a space feel thoughtfully layered and inviting.”—Lindsey Christie, owner and principal designer of Lindsey Grace Interiors.

    "We love to source outdoor chairs from DWR. The Palissade Side Chair is a favorite: It’s a great value, a true workhorse, and its modern lines and colors look just as good indoors as they do on a terrace."—Melissa Hall Simmons, principal of Studio MH.

    #135051. Which Video Game Consoles Are Worth Buying in 2026?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1277 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

    Which Video Game Consoles Are Worth Buying in 2026?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1277 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The video game industry is in a wild place.
    • That’s what I’m here to do, to help you weighs the pros and cons of these (mostly) years old consoles against the current price.
    • In a recent development, the PlayStation 5 is your best entryway into 4K gaming and is the best way to play GTA VI.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The video game industry is in a wild place. The biggest games of the generation are coming out, Grand Theft Auto 6 on Xbox and PlayStation, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. At the same time, hardware has never been more expensive. The cheapest fresh consoles now start at $500, $600 if you want a PS5 (the most popular place to play GTA), with many going for more than that. To top it off with a cherry, Nintendo just hiked the price of its family friendly Switch 2 up to $500, not 18 months after its initial release. So the question now is: if you’re buying a new console in 2026, which ones are actually worth the cost?

    That’s what I’m here to do, to help you weighs the pros and cons of these (mostly) years old consoles against the current price. I personally love my PS5 Pro, but given the current asking price and availability, I would recommend the other, less pricey PS5 models instead to 95 percent of players. If you asked me, two years ago, if you should buy an Xbox Series S or Series S, I’d have a different answer than I do today. And then, there’s handhelds. Do you get a Switch 2 or opt for a beefier PC handheld? I’ll help you figure all that out and more, starting with the PlayStation.

    In a recent development, the PlayStation 5 is your best entryway into 4K gaming and is the best way to play GTA VI. Sony has pulled ahead of Microsoft in terms of exclusive titles with games like Astro Bot, God of War: Ragnarok, and Horizon Forbidden West (and you get access to that amazing PS4 library as well). In terms of tech, the DualSense controller is an impressive leap forward when games take advantage of what it can do. The console technically supports outputs of up to 8K resolution and 120 frames per second on compatible titles. For the most part, though, you'll be playing closer to 4K60—or 4K30 in the case of GTA VI.

    Sources indicate that I've stated it before, and I'll say it again: The PS5 Disc Edition is the best console for most gamers. If you want to play GTA 6 at launch, this is probably what you should get. This edition has a disc drive, so you can pop in physical game discs or watch 4K Blu-rays. Totally worth the $650 asking price, in my opinion.

    If all you’re going to ever play is GTA 6 and never buy a game again, well, you can save yourself a little money and opt for the Digital Edition instead. Even the physical version of the game is just a download code in a box. The Digital Edition comes with a reduced price tag and slightly reduced bulk. No extra space for that disc drive makes it the best-looking PS5 to date. Aside from that, it's virtually identical to the regular PS5 Slim in terms of power and performance.

    Sources indicate that the PS5 Pro is mid-generation upgrade for the gamers who really care, but with things the way they are now, the enhancements are not worth it. Pre-owned Pro consoles are going from between $1,400 and $1,900 at various major box retailers, and you can’t even find latest ones most days.

    Certain titles like Final Fantasy VII Rebirth perform noticeably better on the Pro, and most games get some kind of boost, but it’s certainly not worth double or triple the price of what you’d otherwise be paying. The kicker is that GTA VI doesn’t even have a higher framerate mode on the Pro—it still runs at 30fps, just with fewer dips during chaotic moments as compared to the regular PS5. Even if I wanted to tell you to buy one to play the best version of GTA, I couldn’t.

    On the Microsoft side, the Xbox Series X is the top of the line. This is where I blew through such technical powerhouses as Alan Wake 2 and Senua's Saga: Hellblade 2—two of the best-looking games I've ever played. The problem in 2026 is that, power-wise, the Series X is much closer to a regular PS5 than a PS5 Pro. And, right now, they start at $800. At that point, I’m sorry, there’s no reason not to go PlayStation.

    Sources indicate that if you're looking to play GTA 6 on an Xbox this year, I recommend the Xbox Series S instead. It launched simultaneous to the Series X as the budget alternative and, well, it still is... comparatively. The Series S is smaller, less expensive and sacrifices a disc drive. Unlike with Sony's Digital Edition PS5, there are significant tech differences between these two Xbox Series models. Most notably, it's a native 1440p console. It can upscale games to run at 4K on a 4K TV, but it can't run them natively like the Series X can. Compared to other consoles, GTA runs just as smoothly, with just as much detail thanks to Xbox’s upscaling tech, only at 1080p resolution instead of 4K. It’s another good recommendation for the casual gamer who wants to get a no-frills GTA machine as cheap as possible.

    In a recent development, even with a new Nintendo console coming this year, we can't ignore gaming's most popular option. Revolutionary at the time, this console combined Nintendo's console ambition with the mass appeal of its handhelds in a machine that did both. The Nintendo Switch is still affordable and family friendly, and it's the only place you can legally play Mario games. Exclusive titles like Donkey Kong: Bonanza and the Ocarina of Time remake bolster the existing library and give a reason to upgrade.

    Sources indicate that still, I have a hard time recommending any gamer still happy with their Switch upgrade for the sake of it. The leap just isn’t that monumental. That being mentioned I won’t hesitate to recommend the Switch 2 for anyone newly introduced to the hardware. It’s objectively better and the longevity will be worth the price difference.

    Industry observers note that GTA 6 might not be coming to PC right away, but that isn't a good reason to neglect my personal handheld of choice. Ever since the introduction of the Steam Deck, the PC-gaming market has been going increasingly mobile. And the upgraded OLED model is still the gold standard—trust me, I’ve tried them all.

    My top recommendation for the average console gamer is the Steam Deck OLED. It runs on Valve's SteamOS, so you don't even have to worry about learning Windows (like some kind of PC gamer). The Steam Deck UI completely console-ifies your entire Steam library and makes it easy for newbies to jump in. If you're used to the Switch, you may find it to be a bit beefy, but once I got used to it, I actually found the Steam Deck OLED to be the most ergonomic of all PC-gaming handhelds.

    It's never been a better time to get your feet wet, buy some games on Steam (wait for a sale; there will be plenty), and see what all the fuss is about. If the price looks prohibitive and you don't care much about graphics, get the cheaper LCD model while it's still being sold.

    Here at Esquire, we compile our guides by performing heavy research and testing, and the gadgets we choose to award are what we’d spend our own money on. We choose the best tech for you based on our experience. We know which little details are deal-breakers and can help you separate the nice-to-haves from the needs.
